messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Alvarez, a 36-year-old married tax consultant, came to treatment after years of trying to keep himself functioning by keeping his world narrow and controlled. He described a deployment in which a routine patrol changed in an instant when an improvised blast struck the vehicle ahead of his unit. In the blast’s aftermath, what stayed with him most was not only the sight and sound of the explosion but the bitter, metallic taste in his mouth as he dragged himself through smoke and dust, tasting grit and blood while trying to understand who was still alive. Later, even an ordinary trigger could pull him straight back into that scene: if a conversation at work turned to military losses, or if his wife asked a careful question about what had happened, Daniel felt the memory arrive before he could prepare himself, vivid and immediate as though the patrol were unfolding again in the room with him. The trigger itself was enough to summon the memory; hearing those topics or feeling the pressure of a careful question would drag him back into the blast scene before he had any chance to steady himself. In the first months afterward, certain conversation topics—anything about military losses, injuries, or “what happened over there”—could make his mind snap back to that scene. When the memory came, he said it could hit with such force that he had to stop mid-sentence, overwhelmed by emotion, or else he would feel strangely numb, as if the event belonged to someone else. He had come to dread those returns of memory because they did not arrive as distant recollections; they arrived with the taste, the emotion, and the blunt sense that danger was present again. Because the memory kept returning in that vivid, unfinished way, he began to find new triggers everywhere—brief silences, a hand coming toward his shoulder, the wrong topic raised in conversation, even a shift in tone that reminded him of the seconds before the blast.  

Daniel’s reactions shaped the way he moved through ordinary life. He avoided talking with anyone about the event or its aftermath, and he also pushed away positive feelings when they surfaced, because they felt unsafe and almost naive in the face of what he knew could happen. After a few painful attempts at opening up with his wife, he began changing the subject whenever she asked about his service, and he noticed that even a well-meaning touch on the shoulder could make him recoil. Any form of physical contact with others became something he braced against, and this withdrawal had a quiet but steady effect on his daily life: at home he sat farther from his wife on the couch, and at work he kept his interactions clipped and professional, avoiding casual warmth that might invite more than he could manage. By keeping the topic shut down and pulling away from touch, he found the memory had nowhere to be worked through; it stayed sealed off, and when it did break through it came back in the same raw, fragmentary form he had tried so hard not to face. At the same time, these habits made the event feel even less integrated into his own life. Because he refused to speak about it and worked hard not to feel anything good or soft, the memory remained sealed off, returning in fragments rather than in a fuller narrative. The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close, and when he finally relaxed for a moment the memory surged back with more force, as if all the years of not touching it had left it undigested and intact. When it did return, it often did so through a cue that seemed trivial to others—a certain topic raised in conversation, or the sudden physical sensation of being touched unexpectedly—and the more he shut himself down, the more stark and unbidden those recalls became.  

Over time, Daniel became increasingly watchful. Unusual silence made him feel something dangerous was about to happen, and he would scan a room for exits before he could settle enough to stay. Living with that constant sense of danger made him more likely to notice the smallest hints of possible threat, and those cues began to stand out to him as if they were warnings he could not ignore. Even a quiet pause or a sudden shift in another person’s movement could become a trigger in its own right. Living at that pitch of threat, he started reading almost any small cue as a warning; a quiet conference room at the tax office, a coworker stepping too close, or an unexpected pause in a client dinner could all tip into alarm before anything was actually wrong. That habit was especially obvious in his office and at client dinners, where he sat with his back to the wall and mentally identified escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere. A quiet conference room, a lull in conversation, or a colleague stepping too close could all make his body react as if the threat were immediate. He startled with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly, and that alarm was not random: it was rooted in the way his memory could flare up without warning, carrying the taste of the event and the old certainty that disaster could erupt from calm. In turn, the more he organized his life around avoiding touch, avoiding conversation, and dodging any rush of positive feeling, the less room he allowed for reminders to settle into context. The remembered scene returned in more stripped-down form—sometimes vivid enough that he could taste it again, sometimes numbed out and unreal—and each recurrence made him more alert for danger in the present. He began reading silence as a sign of imminent harm, and he became quicker to notice potential triggers in other people’s words, their tone, or the way they reached toward him.  

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by the narrowing of his life. What brought him in was a recent evening at home when his wife touched his arm in the darkened kitchen and he jerked away hard enough to frighten her, then later found himself overwhelmed by a sudden rush of the memory when a dinner conversation turned to old service stories. He hated that the event could still command him so completely, and he was most afraid that if he kept backing away from contact, from conversation, and from any feeling that seemed too good to trust, he would end up living as if the blast had never ended. The more he organized his days around those protective habits, the more the memory stayed close and the more easily it returned when his guard was down; what he had tried to put at a distance remained vivid and intact. At the same time, he hoped that treatment might help him face the memory without being overtaken by it, and make ordinary closeness with his wife and the rest of his life feel safe again.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers leading to avoidance and withdrawal, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers themselves cause or drive the maladaptive strategies as a causal relationship.
The vignette says triggers summon the memory, but it does not explicitly show the memory causing new triggers in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows the memory producing a sense of threat, but it does not clearly state that the sense of threat leads to the memory returning in a causal way.
The vignette shows threat increasing vigilance and cue detection, but it does not explicitly state that threat causes triggers to arise in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows avoidance and emotional shutdown preserving the memory, but it does not clearly state that the maladaptive strategies lead to the memory in a causal way.
The vignette shows avoidance and withdrawal making Daniel more alert to cues, but it does not clearly state that the maladaptive strategies themselves generate triggers in a causal way.
